case.start.title: Radar saw the eye of {name} through the clouds
case.start.body: On {date}, the NISAR radar satellite (a NASA and ISRO mission) passed over the Bay of Bengal. This was hours before {name} reached land near Narsapur. Clouds hid the storm from normal cameras. Radar can see through cloud, so it caught the eye of the storm.
case.start.hint: Scroll down to go through the story, or pick a chapter at the top.
case.above.title: What a normal camera saw
case.above.body: A camera on a weather satellite took this picture on {date}. Thick cloud covers the sea, so it mostly shows the tops of the clouds, not the water. The line is the cyclone's path, from weather office reports. Each dot is one report.
case.above.key_track: Cyclone path, from weather office reports
case.clouds.title: Radar sees under the clouds
case.clouds.body: Radar sends out its own signal and listens for the echo. Cloud does not stop it. The left side is the calm sea on {before}. The right side is the storm eye on {during}.
case.swipe.label: Drag to compare the calm sea and the storm
case.swipe.hint: Drag the line, or click it and use the left and right arrow keys.
case.rough.title: How much rougher the sea got
case.rough.body: Brighter radar means rougher water. The chart shows how much brighter the storm sea is at each distance from the eye, compared with a calm sea.
case.rough.hint: Move along the chart. The ring on the map moves to the same distance from the eye.
case.rough.chart_title: Rise in radar brightness by distance from the eye
case.rough.chart_unit: Relative dB, where 0 is the calm sea
case.rough.chart_aria: Line chart of brightness rise against distance from the eye, with a shaded uncertainty band
case.rough.fallback: The chart could not load. Dashed rings show 25, 50 and 100 km from the eye.
case.shore.title: The shore: where water may have stayed
case.shore.body: The shore is the flat delta where the storm came ashore. The left side is the coast on {before}. The right side is the newest radar pass, on {after}. Drag the line to compare.
case.classes.title: What the colours mean
case.classes.explain: “Likely” means the radar change points to it. Nobody has checked it on the ground.
case.classes.note: Not a warning. Not a flooded area in km².
case.shore.open_hint: Opens the workspace with the two coast pictures side by side.
case.radar.title: What radar can't show
case.radar.body: Radar is a strong tool, but it has limits. These are four claims people often make. Each one has a verdict based on this data.
case.radar.c1.claim: Radar can see the sea under clouds.
case.radar.c1.why: Radar sends its own signal, so cloud does not stop it. This is how the eye was seen on {date}, while cameras saw only cloud.
case.radar.c2.claim: Radar tells you how fast the wind blows.
case.radar.c2.why: A rougher sea looks brighter, but that is a clue, not a speed. Wind speed in metres per second is not shown here.
case.radar.c3.claim: Radar sees flood water under crops.
case.radar.c3.why: Radar waves can bounce off water under crop stems. But dense crops can hide water, so some floods will be missed.
case.radar.c4.claim: Radar shows the flooded area in km².
case.radar.c4.why: The colours are likely labels from a change threshold. They are not measurements. The app shows shares of each mandal, not an area in km².
case.radar.slider_hint: Wavelength is the distance from one wave crest to the next. Move the slider to compare.
case.radar.slider_aria: Radar wavelength, from 24 centimetres (L-band) to 9 centimetres (S-band)
case.radar.note_l: L-band waves (24 cm) pass through the crop canopy and bounce between water and stems, so flooded fields show up bright.
case.radar.note_s: S-band waves (9 cm) bounce off the canopy, so most flooded fields under crops stay hidden.
case.radar.diagram_alt: Diagram of a radar wave going down toward water under a crop canopy
case.radar.fig_note: This picture shows radar brightness only. It does not show wind speed.
case.about.title: About this story
case.about.intro: This page tells one story with the data in the workspace. Here is where the data came from, how it was made, and what it cannot tell you.
case.about.data_body: Radar pictures come from NASA's NISAR L-band radar (NASA JPL and ISRO, through ASF DAAC). Cloud pictures come from NASA GIBS. The cyclone path is typed in by hand from IMD bulletins.
case.about.methods_body: Radar pictures were cut to the study area and made smaller for the web. They are shown in greys, as brightness, not as measured units. The colours compare two passes on the same track against a threshold. Numbers come with a ± range.
case.about.limit1: Radar does not measure wind speed.
case.about.limit2: Rain and rough sea also make radar brighter, so a bright patch is not always water.
case.about.limit3: Dense crops can hide water from radar.
case.about.limit4: The “likely” colours come from a threshold. They are not a warning, and they are not an area in km².
case.about.limit5: The cyclone path is straight lines between IMD reports, not the true path.
case.about.limit6: IMD is still confirming the landfall time.
case.about.limit7: The eye is small and weak in this radar view (about 5 km core, bright ring near 14 km). The brightness-rise chart compares 27 Oct with a provisional calm scene (15 Oct) that has dark patches, so read its shape, not its level.
case.about.placeholder_body: Some pictures and numbers are sample values for now. Each one has a dashed tag: “Sample values” for numbers, “Quick-look sample” for pictures. The real files will replace them.
